title: Time and space complexity
text: Time complexity describes how the number of operations grows with input size n. A single loop over n elements is O(n); two fully nested loops over n elements are O(n²). Binary search halves the remaining range each step and takes O(log n). Auxiliary space counts extra memory used by the algorithm. A recursive algorithm also uses call-stack space: linear recursion depth needs O(n) stack space. Big-O is an upper bound, not a measured execution time.

title: Hashing and frequency maps
text: Hashing stores values under keys so a frequency map can count repeated elements. For Two Sum, scan the array and look for target minus the current number in a map of earlier values. Check the complement before inserting the current index so an element is not paired with itself. Expected time is O(n) and auxiliary space is O(n). Hash table operations have expected O(1) time with suitable hashing; collisions can degrade worst-case performance.

title: Recursion and backtracking
text: Recursion solves a problem by calling the same function on a smaller state. Define the state, base case, and transition before coding. A base case terminates recursion. Backtracking chooses an option, explores recursively, then undoes the choice so another branch starts from the correct state. Generating all subsets of n elements explores 2^n choices; copying each output subset costs up to O(n), so output construction costs O(n·2^n). The recursion stack uses O(n) space, excluding stored output.

title: Merge sort and quicksort
text: Merge sort divides an array into halves, sorts them recursively, and merges sorted halves. Its recurrence T(n)=2T(n/2)+O(n) gives O(n log n) time and the usual array implementation needs O(n) auxiliary space. Quicksort partitions around a pivot. Balanced partitions give expected O(n log n) time with randomized pivot selection, while consistently poor partitions give O(n²). In-place partitioning still requires recursive stack space.

title: Kadane: maximum subarray sum
text: Kadane's algorithm finds the maximum sum of a contiguous nonempty subarray. Maintain the best sum ending at the current position and the best sum seen overall. For value x, set ending=max(x,ending+x), then best=max(best,ending). Initialize both values with the first element so an all-negative array correctly returns its largest element. Time is O(n), auxiliary space O(1). A subarray must be contiguous; a subsequence can skip elements while preserving their order.

title: Two pointers for a sorted array
text: To find a pair summing to a target in a sorted array, begin with one pointer at each end. If the sum is too small, increase the left pointer; if too large, decrease the right pointer. Sorting makes these moves valid because increasing the left value cannot decrease the sum. Each pointer moves at most n times, so the scan is O(n) with O(1) auxiliary space. If sorting is needed, include its O(n log n) time and preserve original indices when required.

title: Binary search and lower bound
text: Binary search requires an ordered search space or a monotone predicate. For exact search on a sorted array, maintain inclusive low and high bounds; compute mid=low+(high-low)//2. If nums[mid] is smaller than target, set low=mid+1; otherwise move high=mid-1. Return the index when equal. The search takes O(log n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Lower bound returns the first position whose value is greater than or equal to target; using a half-open interval [low,high) and moving high=mid preserves that boundary.

title: Binary search on the answer
text: Binary search on the answer uses a monotone feasibility test. For minimum capacity to ship packages within D days, capacity must be at least the largest package and can be at most the sum of weights. Greedily scan packages in order to count required days for a proposed capacity. If that capacity needs at most D days, search smaller capacities; otherwise increase capacity. The feasibility test is O(n), and the complete algorithm is O(n log R), where R is the search range.

title: Linked list reversal and cycle detection
text: Reverse a singly linked list by storing the next node, redirecting the current node's next pointer to the previous node, then advancing both pointers. This is O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space. Floyd's cycle detection uses a slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two steps. If they meet, a cycle exists; if the fast pointer reaches null, no cycle exists. To find the cycle entry after a meeting, reset one pointer to the head and move both one step until they meet again.

title: Monotonic stack and next greater element
text: A monotonic stack maintains elements or indices in sorted order. To find the next greater element on the right, scan from right to left. Remove stack values that are less than or equal to the current value, read the remaining top as the next greater value, then push the current value. Each element is pushed once and popped at most once, so the total time is O(n), despite the nested while loop. Auxiliary space is O(n). Use indices when positions or distances are required.

title: Sliding window: longest substring without repeats
text: For the longest substring without repeating characters, track the most recent index of each character and maintain a left boundary. At index right with character ch, update left=max(left,last_seen[ch]+1) when ch has been seen, then store last_seen[ch]=right. Update the best length with right-left+1. Taking the maximum prevents the left boundary from moving backward; the string abba is an important test. Each character is processed once: O(n) time and O(min(n,alphabet_size)) space. This is a contiguous substring problem, not a subsequence problem.

title: Heaps, priority queues and top K
text: A heap supports removing the smallest or largest item efficiently. A min-heap keeps its minimum at the root. To retain the k largest numbers from a stream, maintain a min-heap of at most k numbers, inserting each number and removing the minimum if the heap grows larger than k. Processing n elements costs O(n log k), with O(k) auxiliary space. Reading the heap root is O(1); inserting and removing the root are O(log k). A heap is not a fully sorted array.

title: Binary tree traversals
text: Preorder visits root, left subtree, then right subtree. Inorder visits left, root, then right; it yields sorted values for a binary search tree under its ordering rule. Postorder visits left, right, then root, useful when combining child results. Recursive traversal visits each node once, giving O(n) time and O(h) stack space for height h. Level-order traversal uses a queue and visits nodes breadth first; its extra space is proportional to the maximum width of the tree.

title: BFS and DFS graph traversal
text: Breadth-first search (BFS) uses a queue and explores an unweighted graph in layers. Mark a node visited when enqueuing it to avoid duplicate work. BFS finds shortest path length measured in number of edges in an unweighted graph. Depth-first search (DFS) uses recursion or an explicit stack to explore a path before backtracking. With an adjacency list, both traverse O(V+E) work and use O(V) extra space. For disconnected graphs, start a new traversal from each unvisited vertex.

title: Dijkstra shortest paths
text: Dijkstra finds shortest paths from a source in a graph with nonnegative edge weights. Maintain distance estimates and a min-priority queue. Remove the entry with the smallest distance, skip stale entries, and relax each outgoing edge when a shorter path is found. A negative edge invalidates Dijkstra's greedy finalization assumption; use an algorithm such as Bellman-Ford when negative weights are present and handle negative cycles. With a binary heap and adjacency list, time is O((V+E) log V) for a simple graph; distances and graph storage need O(V+E) space.

title: Topological sort and cycle detection
text: A topological ordering places every directed edge u→v with u before v. It exists only for a directed acyclic graph. Kahn's algorithm computes indegrees, enqueues all vertices with indegree zero, removes them one at a time, and decreases neighbors' indegrees. If fewer than V vertices are processed, a directed cycle exists. With adjacency lists, time is O(V+E) and auxiliary space O(V), excluding graph storage. More than one valid topological ordering may exist.

title: Disjoint set union and Kruskal
text: Disjoint set union (DSU) maintains connected components using find and union operations. Path compression redirects visited nodes to their component representative. Union by size or rank keeps trees shallow. The amortized time per operation is O(alpha(n)), which grows extremely slowly. Kruskal's minimum spanning tree algorithm sorts undirected weighted edges and adds an edge only when its endpoints belong to different DSU components. Sorting dominates at O(E log E). A disconnected graph produces a minimum spanning forest.

title: Memoization vs tabulation in dynamic programming
text: Dynamic programming reuses results of overlapping subproblems. Memoization is top-down: start from the original recursive recurrence, cache each state's result, and avoid solving that state again. Tabulation is bottom-up: initialize base cases and fill states in dependency order. Memoization evaluates reachable states and uses a recursion stack; tabulation can avoid recursion and may enable rolling-array space optimization. Both need a well-defined state and transition. Estimate time as the number of states times the work per state. Converting recursion into DP requires identifying repeated states, not merely adding a table.

title: 0/1 knapsack and DP state
text: In 0/1 knapsack, each item can be chosen at most once. Define dp[i][w] as the best value using the first i items with capacity w. Either skip the item or take it if its weight fits, referencing the previous row. With a one-dimensional table, process capacities from large to small so the current item is not reused. Complexity is O(nW) time and O(W) auxiliary space for the optimized version. This is pseudo-polynomial in numerical capacity W. Unbounded knapsack allows repeated choices and typically uses ascending capacities.

title: Distinct subsequences DP
text: Count subsequences of source s that equal target t. Let dp[i][j] count matches of t[:j] in s[:i]. Every source prefix has one way to form the empty target, so dp[i][0]=1; an empty source cannot form a nonempty target. Always allow skipping s[i-1]. If s[i-1]==t[j-1], also include dp[i-1][j-1]. Therefore dp[i][j]=dp[i-1][j]+(dp[i-1][j-1] if characters match else 0). Time is O(len(s)·len(t)). A 1D implementation updates target indices backward and uses O(len(t)) space. The source babgbag and target bag have 5 matches.

title: Tries and prefix search
text: A trie stores strings as paths of characters from a root node. Insert a word by creating missing child nodes and mark the final node as terminal. Exact search requires both the full path and a terminal marker; prefix search only requires the path. Inserting or searching a word of length L takes O(L) time under constant-time child lookup. Space depends on the total inserted characters and the representation of child pointers. A prefix can exist even when it is not itself a stored word.

title: Bit manipulation and XOR
text: XOR has the identities x xor x=0 and x xor 0=x. If every integer appears twice except one, XOR of the whole array yields that single number in O(n) time and O(1) extra space. To test whether a positive integer n is a power of two, check n>0 and (n & (n-1))==0. The expression n & (n-1) removes the lowest set bit. Do not apply the power-of-two test without checking positivity, because zero also satisfies the bit expression.
